I was just reminiscing on the game after listening to the soundtrack. I realized that this was the *only* game to have ever engage the player by thrusting them into a mission. The whole game is more or less turn based except the moments where you get hacked and a timer starts of you having to get a new IP address. The game rest of the game plays out like "Mission: hack this place. No time limit." and you can take your time doing multiple attempts. The crazy twist comes when [spoiler]you get a message from the chat board saying that someone from the group has gone AWOL and you have like 10 minutes to save some people irl.[\spoiler] No other game has you fumbling at your keyboard trying to complete a task like that. Not one. Most games I can put down and never pick up again, but this one has me hacking like there isn't a pause function (I forgot if there even is a pause screen). This game is still in the hall of fame.

I'll admit, I was not expecting much from a free humble game, especially one developed by a single person. Yet, I am plesantly suprised by the gameplay overall. This game is a hacking-puzzle game with a story essentially. 

When it comes to the hacking part, the mechanics feel cool to use and at times when hacking servers it can get intense and the learning curve as a result is well made. 

The puzzle part is also great, the game will tell you what you need to initally do in a mission and what the end goal is, but it heavily relies on your past experience with game mechanics and a bit of snooping on files to navigate through a misson.

The story itself is a 7.5 out of 10 but the story telling is 9 out of 10. To get the story in this game, you'll have to snoop on files like you would do in regular missons, with some files pointing in other directions for more bits of the story and since you are already conditioned to snoop around, the way the story is told fits the context well.

Replayability is quite good, passwords, usernames (non generic ones) and a bunch of information in missions is randomly generated which can be refreshing, but also the game has multiple paths with an obvious linear path and a secretive path which means you'll be going back to the game to find its secrets. 

It also has some humorous parts of the game which did may be giggle a bit.

I only have a couple issues:

- The saving system is a one slot system, so when I was at the point in the story where the secret path can be taken I couldn't make two game saves, and for the sake of the story line I went with the normal path on my first go.
- On some themes (the way the UI is arranged) tags on the map appear to be unreadable due to the names being cut off
- Achievement recognition is buggy, if you are a completionist, better prepare to pull your hair out

The game does make you feel like you know something about coding, but you're still Jon Snow anyway. 
Wouldn't recommend playing anywhere that is concerned with security, or you will probably be taken in for questioning. Nope, don't want that. 

10/10 for how the game works, but I wish it had more contracts and harder contracts while make you sweat.

I saw that this was free on Humble Bundle and thought "what the heck", and proceeded to download and play it. I'm glad I did.

Unlike the movies, or even some games, where hacking looks so easy that even a toddler can do it, Hacknet has the decency to make you work for it. While many elements are simplified, the game still has you using actual command prompt commands to get through the game, and a Computer Science major such as myself appreciates that kind of accuracy.

The game isn't all that hard, with the biggest obstacles you encounter are time-pressure missions that can screw you over if you're not a quick typer. There's also a RAM mechanic that keeps you from running too many processes at one time. While I appreciate the accuracy to real life, nobody has less than 1 GB RAM in 2018. That's absurd.

The story's pretty interesting. A hacker's dead, you go about uncovering the circumstances behind it, and a lot of the missions tend to be congruent with pertinent issues on computer security in this day and age. My hope is that people who play this game become aware of these serious issues, and that a few misconceptions about hackers and hacking in general are disproven.

An unexpected highlight for me was the music. I got the soundtrack along with this game, and I enjoyed it so much, I'm probably adding it to my playlist for when I'm coding something.

Overall, I recommend playing this game. It doesn't take long to beat, and you'll feel like a real Guy in the Chair while playing through.

When I first started playing this game I assumed it was just another boring story game...I didn't realise how wrong I was. Hacknet is so much more than a story game, it is a logical puzzle game, sci-fi, simulation, Hacking and more. The thing that made it for was the incorporation of real commands that are used for 'real' hacking, this feature connects this game to everyday life and really makes it shine. This is also complemented by the story which helps make the game not repetitive and progressively harder as you go along. 

The only thing that I can critique this game on is the few spelling/grammar mistakes I found along the way, but this is hardly a critique and more human error. 

I give this game a 9.5/10 for its wonderful story, incorporation of real-world aspects and the desire to keep playing.

At first. I thought this game was just an indie game with no story about hacking various computers like a never ending dungeon. I was mistaken.

When I first saw Mutahar play this game in one of his videos, I was interested but I didn't look into it much after that. It was only until a few days ago (at the time of writing) I saw it was for free on the Humblebundle store. So I picked it up. I blazed through the tutorial and I started doing contracts. Got hacked myself but for the most part, everything went flawlessly.

I won't spoil one of the contracts. But that was the turning point. It's one of the last contracts and it took me a while to figure out the answer, but when I did, my heart sank. Got a few emails and decided to continue on with the story. And with any game with a story, I won't spoil the ending if it's justified. And it's justified.

The music is amazing. At the end, I felt like I was going to shed a tear. During the bulk of the game (which is just doing contracts for people.) some chill music plays. And at the final hack, it's intense. I'd say on par with Simon Viklund of Payday fame. Christopher Larkin, hats off to you. You did an amazing job with the soundtrack.

The gameplay, while repetitious, kept me engaged. I felt like a cyber god hacking into what many called "unhackable". That was enough to keep me going.

Is the game worth it on the story alone? No. I'd say not. The story doesn't come in at full force at about around the halfway mark. The first tidbit you get of it is that the first guy you talk to is dead. 

Is the game fun? That depends. If you can get past typing the first few letters of something and pressing tab and getting past firewalls, I'd say yeah. But if you can't, then this game isn't for you.

Was the game worth my time? Absolutely.

Is the game worth $10 if you can get past the repetition? Yes.

Is it worth buying during a sale? Absolutely.

As a former sysadmin geek, I approve this!

If you ever wondered how a Unix like system works and wanted to be felt like a security expert, go no further. Although very simplified compared to the real thing, it is very well done and you will not regret getting this.

It skipps the boring parts of an admins life (analyzing errpt lines and ODM issues all day are not so fun, after all) and moves in to the exciting world of a hacker. Tools, procedures and even services with proper port numbers are mimicking the real world in the game, with some well done missions and a great story.

I only miss few things, like a multiplayer mode and hardware upgrades (what we had in Uplink many Years ago), but overall it's a great game.
